  ```{r, echo=T, results='asis'}
require(glmnet); require(ggplot2)
require(Hmisc); require(remotes)
# remotes::install_github("tomwenseleers/L0glm/L0glm")
require(L0glm);
devtools::load_all(".")

require(ordinis); require(ncvreg)

# 2019 05
# To show the volatility of selected features using Monte Carlo simulation.  A setup could be like this:

# N=500, p=500 candidate features.  The 500 features are Bernoulli with prob.=1/10 and the regression coefficients are standard normal (500 random values, only create one and keep using for all simulations.  Likewise use the same binary predictors over all simulations).  Compute X*beta and rescale it to have a range from -3 to 3.  Generate binary Y from a logistic model with this rescaled vector of linear predictors.   Repeat  500 times.  Make a scatterplot with 500 points showing x=rescaled beta, y=proportion of the 500 simulations in which that variable was selected by lasso.
```



```{r, echo=T, results='asis'}

NOBS <- 5000   # N=500
NP <- 500     #500 candidate features
pr <- 0.1     #500 features are Bernoulli with prob.=1/10
simu <-100   #500 simulations.

dist <- 'laplace'
# Shi - suggest changing file name to not have laplace in the name but use
# same script for two purposes

set.seed(1234)

# Creat features matrix
X <- matrix(rbinom(NOBS*NP, 1, prob=pr), ncol=NP)

# betas (before rescaling) sampled from the kind of distribution that is what the lasso is optimized for: 
# the Laplace or double exponential exp(-abs(u)) density. 

rlaplace <-    # from OOmisc package
  function(n,beta){
    if(beta<=0) stop("Beta should be positive") 
    u=runif(n)
    print(u)
    ifelse(u<0.5,beta*log(2*u),-beta*log(2*(1-u)))
  }

Coef <- switch(dist,
               normal  = rnorm(NP),
               laplace = rlaplace(NP, 1) )  # location 0 dispersion 1

summary(Coef)

L.val <- X %*% Coef     # Creat Linear Predictor   


summary(L.val)

#rescale L.val to have quantile range from -3 to 3: 
# Change range of L.val from -3 to 3 to -5 to 5.
# find a and b such that a*X*beta + b has desired range

r <- quantile(L.val, c(.025, .975))
# a <- 6 / diff(r)
# b <- 3 - a * r[2]


# a <- 10 / diff(r)
# b <- 5 - a * r[2]

# rescale to -4 to 4

a <- 8 / diff(r)
b <- 4 - a * r[2]


a;b

L.val.scaled <- a * L.val + b


summary(L.val.scaled)

# Re-scale Coef accordingly

# Coef <- a * Coef + b

#The linear predictor needed to have its intercept adjusted 
#so the overall mean is near zero. But the coefficients are adjusted 
#for the #intercept and don't need that addition.

Coef <- a * Coef 

summary(Coef)

# Run simu simulations, each first creat Y.val, then conduct cv.glmet.
# v matrix is 0/1 depending on the variable selected for the run
# corresponding to the row of v


# For each iteration store the C-index computed from the theoretical logit and the observed Y:


vs <- matrix(0, nrow=simu, ncol=NP)
ys <- matrix(0, nrow=simu, ncol=1)
cs <- matrix(0, nrow=simu, ncol=1)

# simu replications
for(i in 1:simu){ 
  
  print(i)
  
  ## Shi: set.seed(i)  don't reset again
  
  Y.val <- ifelse(runif(500)<=plogis(L.val.scaled), 1, 0)
  
  ys[i, ] <-sum(Y.val)
  
  cs[i, ] <-somers2(L.val.scaled, Y.val)['C']
  
  ## Shi see if cv.glmnet accepts a 0/1 variable instead of factor
  
  y1 <-factor(Y.val, levels = c(0,1), labels=c("no", "yes"))  # predicting binary Y.
  
  ## Shi make sure the coefficients are estimated from the whole sample, not from cross-validation - YES NOW THAT WAS NOT CORRECT - COEFS WERE NOT ESTIMATED FROM WHOLE DATASET
  
  # cv.glmmod <- cv.glmnet(X, (y1=="yes")*1, alpha=1, family=c("binomial"),type.measure="deviance",intercept=T)
  # # deviance is the most sensitive method so let's go with that
  #   # plot(cv.glmmod)
  # # FIXED: estimate coefficients from whole dataset & only use CV to determine optimal lambda
  # fit.glmmod <- glmnet(X, (y1=="yes")*1, alpha=1,
  #                      family=c("binomial"),
  #                      intercept=T)
  # reg.coef = predict(fit.glmmod, type = "coefficients", s = cv.glmmod$lambda.min)
  # print(range(reg.coef[1]))
  # print(range(reg.coef[-1]))
  
  # cv.ordinis <- cv.ordinis(x=X, y=(y1=="yes")*1, alpha=1,
  #                          penalty="mcp",
  #                          gamma = 1.1, # default 1.4 for mcp, 3.7 for scad
  #                          type.measure = "deviance",
  #                          intercept = TRUE, family = "binomial")
  # # estimate coefficients from whole dataset & only use CV to determine optimal lambda
  # fit.ordinis <- ordinis(x=X, y=(y1=="yes")*1, alpha=1,
  #                          penalty="mcp",
  #                          gamma = 1.1, # default 1.4 for mcp, 3.7 for scad
  #                          intercept = TRUE, family = "binomial")
  # reg.coef = predict(fit.ordinis, type = "coefficients", s = cv.ordinis$lambda.min)
  
  # cv_ncvreg <- cv.ncvreg(X=X, y=(y1=="yes")*1, alpha=1,
  #                          penalty="SCAD",
  #                          # gamma = 3.7, # default 3 for mcp, 3.7 for scad
  #                          nfolds = 5,
  #                          family = "binomial")
  # fit_ncvreg <- ncvreg(X=X, y=(y1=="yes")*1, alpha=1,
  #                          penalty="SCAD",
  #                          # gamma = 3.7, # default 3 for mcp, 3.7 for scad
  #                          family = "binomial")
  # reg.coef = predict(fit_ncvreg, type = "coefficients", lambda = cv_ncvreg$lambda.min)
  lambda_preset <- preset.lambda(IC = "bic", # options aic, bic, gic, ebic, mbic 
                                  y = (y1=="yes")*1, 
                                  X = cbind(1, X), 
                                  family = binomial(logit)) 
# preset lambda to optimise given IC in iterative adaptive ridge L0 glm algo
  reg.coef = L0glm.fit(X=Matrix(cbind(1, X), sparse=T), 
                       y=(y1=="yes")*1, 
                               family = binomial(logit), 
                               lambda = lambda_preset, 
                               nonnegative = FALSE,
                               no.pen = 1, # do not penalize intercept
                               normalize = F,
                               start = rep(0.1, ncol(X)+1), # reg.coef, # rep(0.1, ncol(X)+1), # rep(1, ncol(X)+1), # coefficient starting values
                               solver = "eigen", # solver to use
                               method = 7L, # Cholesky
                               thresh = 1E-20,
                               control.solver = modifyList(do.call("control.solver.gen", 
                                                        list(solver = "eigen", 
                                                             method = 7L)), 
                                                list(rowaug=TRUE)) 
                       )$coefficients
  
  vs[i, ] <- ifelse(reg.coef[-1] == 0, 0, 1)  # -1 excludes intercept (assume is first)
}

#Make a scatterplot with NP points showing x=rescaled beta, y=proportion of the simu simulations in which that variable was selected by MCP.

psel <- apply(vs, 2, mean)
```

```{r, echo=T}

s2 <- data.frame(Coef, psel)

ggplot(s2, aes(x=Coef, y=psel)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, span = 0.5, size = 0.5)+ xlab("Real Regression Coefficient")+
  ylab("Proportion Selected")+ylim(0,1)

#The distribution is what we are looking for.  You could use nclass=10 to cut down on noise.

hist(plogis(L.val.scaled), nclass=10)

#make a histogram of these c-indexes

hist(cs[, 1], ylab = "Count", xlab = "c-index", main="")


# save results in an R data file
res <- list(vs=vs, s2=s2, L.val.scaled=L.val.scaled, ys=ys, cs=cs)
save(res, file='res.rda', compress=TRUE)
```
